David I. Meiselman

1924 – 2014 · Economist

A monetarist in the Chicago tradition — student, coauthor, and lifelong defender of Milton Friedman — who spent five decades making one argument wherever Washington would listen: inflation is caused by too much money, and only money can stop it. He chaired a president-elect's task force on inflation, testified before Congress for a quarter-century, and wrote the book that taught the yield curve to speak.

§ 1

About

Boston-born, Chicago-trained, and unmoved by fashion for fifty years.

David I. Meiselman was born in Boston in 1924 and took his bachelor's degree at Boston University in 1947. At the University of Chicago he earned his M.A. in 1951 and his Ph.D. in 1961, studying under Milton Friedman. His dissertation, The Term Structure of Interest Rates, won a Ford Foundation award and was published in 1962; it gave the expectations theory of the yield curve its first clean empirical test. From 1958 to 1962 he was an assistant professor at Chicago, teaching graduate money and running the money-and-banking workshop alongside Friedman.

In 1962 he went to Washington as an economist in the Treasury's Office of Financial Analysis, working under Paul Volcker. He left in May 1963 after refusing political directives that conflicted with honest economics — a pattern that defined his career. He served as senior economist to the House Committee on Banking and Currency under Chairman Wright Patman, lectured at Johns Hopkins, and spent 1964–66 as economist and acting editor of the National Banking Review at the Comptroller of the Currency. In 1963, he and Friedman published “The Relative Stability of Monetary Velocity and the Investment Multiplier” — a 104-page, 215-equation study that became a landmark of the Keynesian–monetarist debates.

From 1966 to 1971 he was F. R. Bigelow Professor of Economics and director of the Bureau of Economic Studies at Macalester College. In December 1968, President-elect Richard Nixon named him chairman of the Task Force on Inflation; its report — monetary and fiscal restraint, pointedly no wage-price controls — was one of six that Arthur Burns forwarded to Nixon as too important to summarize. In 1971 Meiselman moved to Virginia Tech, where he founded the graduate economics department at its Reston branch and taught until 1997. All the while he returned to Washington as a witness, testifying on money, deficits, and inflation into the mid-1990s. He died in Baltimore on December 3, 2014.

§ 3

The Ideas

The arguments he returned to, in testimony, print, and debate, for five decades.

Money growth drives inflation

The core claim of his career, documented across centuries of price history: sustained inflation is always a monetary phenomenon.

“Every substantial and sustained inflation ever studied… has been associated with correspondingly substantial and sustained large-scale increases in the stock of money.”

— David Meiselman, 1969

Deficits don't cause inflation — money does

The Federal Reserve blamed deficits for inflationary money growth. Meiselman checked the data, in the Wall Street Journal, and found the link wasn't there.

“Although the Fed blames deficits for causing inflationary money growth, the evidence is that, from 1960 to 1980, there was no significant relationship between changes in money supply and changes in the national debt.”

— “Deficits, Money, and the Cause of Inflation,” Wall Street Journal, July 21, 1981

Only surprise money moves the real economy

Anticipated money growth is priced in. It is the unanticipated kind that shifts interest rates, output, and employment — the engine of the business cycle.

“It is unanticipated money growth that alters interest rates and the real variables that cause real effects, including business cycles.”

— David Meiselman, Cato Journal, 1986

First, do no harm

Asked what monetary policy should aim at, Meiselman inverted the question: the realistic goal is to stop policy itself from being the problem.

“The best attainable goal of monetary policy is to avoid the problems caused by poor monetary policy.”

— Testimony, House Subcommittee on Domestic Monetary Policy, 1976

Inflation is a hidden tax

Inflation silently pushed taxpayers into higher brackets — bracket creep — raising revenue without a single vote. Washington, he argued in 1982, had “a very strong vested interest in maintaining inflation.”

“More jobs, higher real incomes and lower inflation, especially in the months immediately preceding an election, are widely understood to benefit incumbents.”

— “The Political Monetary Cycle,” Wall Street Journal, January 10, 1984

The yield curve is made of expectations

His 1962 book: long-term interest rates are averages of expected future short rates. Expectations can't be observed directly — so he studied how investors revised them when they were wrong, and showed the revisions move the curve.

“Anticipations may not be realized yet still determine the structure of rates in the manner asserted by the theory.”

— The Term Structure of Interest Rates, Prentice-Hall, 1962, p. 12

A lender of last resort that shouldn't exist

In 1984 Meiselman argued that the Federal Reserve's lender-of-last-resort role — rescuing institutions like Franklin National while money growth lurched — treats symptoms instead of the disease. Under a steady money-supply rule, the function itself becomes unnecessary: stable money, not micro-bailouts, is what prevents panics.

“The only way to stop inflation is to stop the excessive monetary growth which generates the inflation.”

— David Meiselman, The Advocates debate, 1979

Oral History Interview, 1995

Meiselman looks back over his whole career with economist Robert Hetzel — Chicago, Friedman, Treasury, Nixon, and how a course on socialist planning made him a free-marketeer.

Interview highlights
  • “I came there as a truth seeker, you know? After all my years at the University of Chicago.”
    On joining the Treasury in fall 1962, in the Office of Financial Analysis under Paul Volcker. He quit in May 1963 after refusing political directives.
  • His Treasury paycheck read “exchange stabilization fund” — “a giant slush fund,” he joked.
  • “If that's the strongest case, there's no case.”
    On reading Oskar Lange's essay on socialist economics — the reading that made him a lifelong free-marketeer.
  • “Every single one of us had voted republican in 1960. But Patman didn't care about that.”
    On the 1963 House Banking Committee under Chairman Wright Patman, whose monetary crusade he called “a diversion.”
  • “I still miss him. I miss him a lot… when he died, it left a hole on the hill that has never — nobody's replaced him.”
    On Bob Weintraub.
  • “Arthur Burns gave Nixon what Nixon wanted.”
    And: “Milton once told me that Burns was the biggest disappointment of his life.”
  • “I was the chairman of the task force on inflation.”
    On the Nixon transition, meeting at the Hotel Pierre, where Alan Greenspan arrived as Burns's fixer.

Interview · March 28, 1995 · Audio + full transcript · FRASER

Listen & read at FRASER

The Mac Weekly Archive

Macalester's student newspaper mentions Meiselman eleven times between 1966 and 1982 — including his 1982 return lecture arguing money growth should reach zero by 1985.

All 11 mentions, 1966–1982
  • Sept. 9, 1966, p.1 — New-faculty announcement: named F. R. Bigelow professor of economics and director of the Bureau of Economic Studies, succeeding Dr. Arthur Upgren. Full career recap: Ph.D. University of Chicago 1961; instructor, Illinois Institute of Technology; assistant professor, University of Chicago; economist in the office of the Secretary of the U.S. Treasury; senior economist on the House Committee on Banking and Currency; lecturer in political economy at Johns Hopkins 1963–64; economist and acting editor of National Banking Review, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 1964–66.
  • Oct. 7, 1966, p.6 — His Wednesday-noon luncheon course “How to Read the Financial Pages for Fun and Profit” (Student Union rooms 107/108/109; bag lunches invited; first meeting Oct. 12).
  • Oct. 28, 1966, p.6 — The noon course moved to rooms C-2 and C-3 in the new dining hall.
  • Nov. 4, 1966, p.4 — International Conference calendar: Nov. 6, 9:30 p.m., “The British Pound: World Concern for a Nation's Dilemma” — discussion led by Drs. Meiselman and Weekly.
  • Mar. 10, 1967, p.4 — Feature profile “Econ Comes Alive Under Bureau” (Dick Paronto), with a photo of Meiselman at his desk. He revived the dormant Bureau of Economic Studies in fall 1966. “The bureau largely reflects the character of the man who heads it.” Student research topics: money/interest-rate relationships, interest rates and the business cycle, monetary factors in the Argentine and Brazilian inflations. Honors students ran the college computer, analyzed the Economic Report of the President, and their findings were forwarded to the staff of the Joint Economic Committee in Washington.
  • Sept. 22, 1967, p.1 — On Sept. 12 he took six economics majors to a Minneapolis marketing conference on the new input-output table (students: Lew Beccone, Dave Estenson, Bill Miller, Ross Dahlin, Mark Westra, Rick Heuser).
  • Oct. 11, 1968, p.2 — Career notice: Oct. 15, 4:30 p.m., Meiselman and Paul Aslanian spoke on graduate schools of business.
  • Feb. 13, 1970, p.3 — Panel moderator, “Aid and Development” symposium, Feb. 23, Cochran Lounge; key speaker Edward Hamilton (VP, Brookings); panelists William Rogers, Vernon W. Ruttan, John Buttrick (all U. of Minnesota).
  • Mar. 6, 1970, p.1 — Among conservative faculty filibustering a curriculum-revision proposal (“Prominent in this filibuster were Professors Sandburg, Clark, Bunting, Meiselman, Caponi and Donovan”).
  • Apr. 30, 1971, p.3 — Departure: five faculty resignations; economics “suffered the greatest losses: Professors David Meiselman, Paul Aslanian, and Yutaka Horiba.” Meiselman left to start a new graduate department of economics at Virginia Tech's Reston, Virginia branch. “A leading monetarist, Meiselman headed a Nixon Task Force on Inflation in 1968.”
  • Dec. 3, 1982, p.2 — “Speaker slashes Reagan policy 'hoax'” (Andrew Wolfe), headshot by Rob Seckinger. His first return to the college: lecture “Economic Policies and Interest Rates: Reconciling Supply-Side, Keynesian, and Monetarist Views.” He argued “general agreement between the monetarist and supply-side approaches,” called Keynesian analysis “simply wrong,” proposed zero money growth by 1985 (“approximately consistent with zero inflation”), said the federal government “has a very strong vested interest in maintaining inflation” via bracket creep, and called Reagan's deficit concern “a hoax” and a “swindle” if taxes rose without real spending cuts.

From the Archive

His July 21, 1981 Wall Street Journal essay, reproduced in full from the public record.

Deficits, Money, and the Cause of Inflation

By David I. Meiselman

Originally published
The Wall Street Journal, July 21, 1981
Reprinted in
Congressional Record, Vol. 127, Extensions of Remarks, July 24, 1981, pp. 17426–17427
Inserted by
Hon. Clarence J. Brown of Ohio
Source
govinfo.gov — Congressional Record (Bound Edition), 1981, pt. 13

The text below is the Congressional Record reprint, a public record, reproduced verbatim — including Rep. Brown's remarks introducing it.

From the Congressional Record, July 24, 1981 — remarks of Hon. Clarence J. Brown of Ohio:

Mr. Speaker, I would like to place in the RECORD an extremely thoughtful and relevant article by Dr. David I. Meiselman, entitled "Deficits, Money, and the Causes of Inflation." Dr. Meiselman clearly shows in this article that inflation is not caused by tax cuts but by excessive money creation relative to the supply of goods in the economy. The importance of this message is that the claim that the administration's across-the-board marginal tax rate cuts will lead to inflation has absolutely no basis in fact. This article instructs those who oppose the administration's tax plan to instead turn a watchful eye to the Federal Reserve if they are serious about reducing inflation. I recommend this excellent article for my colleagues:

[From the Wall Street Journal, July 21, 1981]

The conventional wisdom holds that budget deficits are a major cause of inflation. Many fiscal conservatives and Keynesians, both liberal and Wall Street varieties, may not agree on very much, but they see eye to eye that deficits mean rising prices. Contrary to these widely and deeply held beliefs, the evidence is that there is little, if any, direct historical connection between budget deficits and inflation, or between deficits and money growth that causes inflation. I ran statistical tests to see if there has been any sizable or dependable relationship between inflation and deficits, tax rates or government expenditures, especially after making allowances for the effects of money supply and output. I found little or no relationship between inflation and the key fiscal policy variables Keynesians believe cause rising prices. I recently reported some of these findings in testimony before the Joint Economic Committee and the Senate Finance Committee. Many other researchers have come to similar conclusions for at least the past 20 years since a pioneering study by Milton Friedman and me first found that the Keynesian analysis that emphasizes deficits is useless in explaining economic events. If deficits don't cause inflation, what does? Inflation follows the general laws of supply and demand. Prices on average increase when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply.

Output Depends on Incentives

Aggregate demand is determined by the quantity of money. There is a close and dependable connection between the nominal quantity of money and nominal gross national product, which is the best measure of total spending, or demand. The quantity of money is controlled by Federal Reserve actions. Aggregate supply depends on other factors, such as available inputs of labor, capital and raw materials, and the state of technology. Output also depends crucially on the incentives to put these means to efficient use. Prices, then, depend on the ratio of money to output. This is a convenient way to summarize aggregate demand and supply. When money grows faster than output, aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply. The result: Prices and interest rates rise, and inflation results. When money and output grow at the same pace, demand and supply remain in balance, and prices on average are stable. The relationship between money per unit of output and inflation may well be the most extensively tested proposition in all of economics with few, if any, exceptions. To reduce inflation, public policies must lead either to more output or to less money growth. Because tax reductions that enhance incentives, such as those in the administration's tax package, lead to more output, the result is lower prices when money is held constant. Reduction in government expenditures also tends to be anti-inflationary. Resources are typically more productive in private sector use, so that reduced government outlays make possible further gains in useful output. In addition, many government programs and transfer payments impair incentives. This analysis also explains why countries such as Japan and Germany, where deficits are a significantly higher fraction of GNP than the U.S., have slower inflation, more growth, more saving, lower nominal interest rates and higher real interest rates than in the U.S. Money has increased more slowly and smoothly in those two countries than in the U.S., and neither country taxes saving and investment as severely as we do. All deficits are not alike, even when they are the same size. It makes a big difference how the deficit is financed. It also makes a difference how the deficit is incurred—whether the deficit is the result of cutting taxes or increasing expenditures, and whether the taxing and spending changes alter total output. Deficits can be financed by selling bonds to the Federal Reserve or to the public. If a deficit is financed by selling government bonds to the Federal Reserve, the resulting increase in the money supply leads to inflation and thereby to rising market interest rates. Alternatively, if the deficit is financed by selling bonds to the public, no such inflationary increase in money takes place. To be sure, real interest rates may rise in order to induce the public to buy the additional bonds. But unless there is an increase in inflation, this rise in interest rates is bound to be small. The major factor causing high interest rates is the large inflation premium which is built into all interest rates at present. Thus, any attempt to lower interest rates by simply printing new money to buy additions to the national debt ends up by causing higher inflation, which, in turn, causes interest rates to rise, not fall. Even though deficit itself may not cause inflation, deficits would lead to inflation if deficits caused the Fed to increase the money supply. Deficits are widely seen as placing some great and large unspecified "burden" on the Federal Reserve. To lighten this burden, the Fed prints some new money and goes out and buys itself some bonds. The Fed is not required by law to monetize the deficit. Indeed, the spirit of the law explicitly prohibits the Fed from doing so; witness the restrictions on direct sales of securities by the Treasury to the Fed. But there is a loophole. The loophole is that the Fed can buy outstanding debt rather than new debt. Because there is essentially no difference between buying old bonds and new bonds, the results of buying old debt are the same as monetizing new debt. When this happens, money expands. Inflation results. Although the Fed often blames deficits for causing inflationary money growth, the evidence is that, from 1960 to 1980, there was no significant relationship between changes in money supply and changes in the national debt. Not only is there no legal or practical need to monetize increases in the public debt, the Fed has not systematically done so. In addition, in recent months high officials of the administration have repeatedly stated that they do not wish the Fed to monetize deficits. The inflation impact of deficits also depends on how they are incurred. The effects of taxes and expenditures are not necessarily offsetting or homogeneous. What is crucial is the impact of taxes and expenditures on output. For example, if deficits occur because of increased government expenditures, these outlays typically use up resources and leave fewer resources for the private sector. Because resources are generally used less efficiently in the public sector, efficiency falls. Even if the same number of people are at work, total output is less useful, less valuable. This is the equivalent of a fall in output, and thereby more inflation. Different tax changes may have different impacts on output. Tax-rate reductions that lessen the disincentive effects of the tax system will cause output to increase. For a given stock of money, more output results in lower prices. Thus, incentive-enhancing tax reduction leads to lower prices, even if the tax cut increases deficits. This is why the administration's tax-reduction package will help to curb inflation, whatever its impact on deficits. Because tax reduction is combined with substantial expenditure cuts, the administration's fiscal package has a significant anti-inflationary impact.

Depressing Private Sector

There is certainly an important and legitimate role for taxes in financing needed government services. If more resources are to be channeled into the public sector, higher taxes depress private sector activity, thereby freeing resources and making them available to the public sector. However, tax rates have already become so high, largely because effective rates have been driven up by bracket creep rather than being explicitly legislated by Congress, that the private sector is already too depressed for our own good. Moreover, the depressive effects of high and rising marginal tax rates have curtailed savings, capital formation and risk-taking more than consumption, and reduced work effort more than leisure. Small wonder that a high employment peacetime economy has little or no growth in recent years for the first time in American history. High levels of taxes do not reduce prices and do not fight inflation. High taxes do reduce output, employment and economic growth. Balancing the budget by squelching initiative and limiting rewards cannot improve our situation. It is time to stop punishing ourselves in the erroneous belief that slow economic growth and recession resulting from excessively high tax rates are the remedy for inflation and high interest rates, or in the hope that pain, itself, will cure our problems. Masochism is not the remedy. Budget cuts, tax cuts that lessen disincentives, regulatory reform and above all a slow, stable and predictable rate of growth of money are the necessary components and the solution for our serious inflation and high interest rate ills. It is time to stop imposing failed remedies on a sick economy.

Archive & Further Reading

Where the papers, records, and primary sources live.

  • FRASER Oral History Collection

    The 1995 interview with Robert L. Hetzel — full transcript (PDF) and audio, held by the Federal Reserve Archival System for Economic Research.

  • Nixon Library — Task Force Finding Aid

    The finding aid for the pre-presidential task force reports, including the 1968 Task Force on Inflation report Meiselman chaired.

  • The David Meiselman Prize

    An annual prize for Macalester economics seniors, still awarded in his name; his name is on the department's awards wall.

  • Wikipedia

    The biographical entry for David I. Meiselman, with references to his major works.

  • The Memorial Book

    David I. Meiselman Memorial Book, 2nd ed., CreateSpace, 2015 — 34 pages, ISBN 978-1511947664. Contributors: Edwin Feulner, Barbara & Stuart Rosenstein, Chaim Meiselman, Roger Waud, Joseph Cole, Henry Cassidy, Edward Nelson, and Robert Auerbach. It covers The Term Structure of Interest Rates (1962) and the Friedman collaboration “The Relative Stability of Monetary Velocity and the Investment Multiplier in the United States, 1897–1958.”

    View on Google Books (no preview available).

  • @MeiselmanEcon on X

    His verified words, posted daily — quotes, testimony, and findings from the archive, each with its source.

  • The David Meiselman Collection on Substack

    The daily long-form article series, with narration, covering one piece of his work at a time.

  • Major Works

    The Term Structure of Interest Rates (1962) · “The Relative Stability of Monetary Velocity and the Investment Multiplier” with Milton Friedman (1963) · The Measurement of Corporate Sources and Uses of Funds with Eli Shapiro (1964) · Varieties of Monetary Experience (1970) · The Phenomenon of Worldwide Inflation, co-edited (1975).

  • Karl Egge Oral History (Macalester, 2006)

    Meiselman and Robert Bunting conducted Egge's job interview at Macalester.

  • Boston Fed — Nantucket Conference Proceedings

    Conference proceedings (~1970; PDF): Meiselman on a panel with Paul Samuelson and Allan Meltzer.

  • The Phenomenon of Worldwide Inflation (AEI, 1975)

    Co-edited with Arthur Laffer; published by the American Enterprise Institute.

  • The Philadelphia Society

    Meiselman was president of the Society 1973–75 and a trustee 1972–86; he chaired a 1979 panel with David Friedman.

  • Virginia House Resolution 294 (2015)

    A memorial resolution honoring him as a “distinguished economist” — Army WWII veteran; B.A. Boston University; M.A. 1951 / Ph.D. 1961, University of Chicago.

  • George Mason University Archives

    No dedicated David Meiselman papers collection exists at George Mason. His materials appear in the Clark E. Warburton papers (the “Meiselman and Simpson” file) and the James Buchanan papers.

  • Open Research Notes

    Items the archive is still tracking down:

    • 1974: “In Defense of Floating Rates: U.S. Inflation Must Be Labelled 'Made In The U.S.' Rather Than 'Imported,'” Wall Street Journal, September 13, 1974 — title verified in Schuettinger & Butler, Forty Centuries of Wage and Price Controls (Heritage Foundation, 1979), p. 177. An “August 23, 1974” entry appears to be a misdated duplicate. Full text not yet recovered.
    • 1977: “Welfare or 'Workfare'?” — Wall Street Journal, November 1977 (exact date unknown). Full text not yet public.
    • Nixon Task Force on Inflation report: full text held only at the Nixon Library Research Room, Yorba Linda; the other five task-force members are not publicly named.
    • Philadelphia Society 1975 presidential address audio: not found anywhere public.
    • Congressional hearing recordings, 1969–1995: written transcripts exist; no audio or video found.
    • Full 1979 Advocates episode: only a 13:20 segment is public.

The David Meiselman Archive is maintained by his grandson, who is compiling the complete record of his writings, testimony, and recordings. Every quotation on this page is reproduced with its source; nothing here is paraphrased into his mouth.
